cards.explanation: The answer is Gad. The LORD asks about Milcom, the god of the Ammonites, “Why then has Milcom taken possession of Gad?” Gad was one of Jacob's sons (Genesis 35:26), and the LORD's first question is “Has Israel no sons?” That's a lot like finding a stranger sitting in a chair with your name on it, and the LORD wants to know why.

The answer is a heap of ruins. The LORD says Rabbah “…will become a heap of ruins, and its villages will be burned.” I think this is one of the heavy parts, friends. It's the LORD speaking about a real city and a real judgment, and the passage doesn't soften it.

The answer is True. After Rabbah falls, the LORD says, “Then Israel will drive out their dispossessors, says the LORD.” The ones who pushed Israel out will be the ones pushed out. It's a turnaround, and this verse puts it in the LORD's own words.

The answer is his priests and officials. The LORD says, “…Milcom will go into exile together with his priests and officials.” So the god and the ones named with him go into exile together. The verse names priests and officials, and no one else.

The answer is riches. The LORD says to the faithless daughter, “You trust in your riches and say, ‘Who can come against me?’” That's a big question to ask when your trust is in your money. I've been guilty of trusting my own stamp work too much, and it never ends well.

The answer is False. The verse says, “You will each be driven headlong, with no one to regather the fugitives.” Nobody is waiting to round them up. That makes the promise coming in verse 6 stand out all the more.

The answer is that the LORD will restore the Ammonites from captivity. He says, “Yet afterward I will restore the Ammonites from captivity…” All that heavy talk, and then one little word turns it. Friends, that “Yet” is doing some serious lifting.

The answer is turn and run and lie low. The LORD says, “Turn and run! Lie low, O dwellers of Dedan, for I will bring disaster on Esau at the time I punish him.” That's a plain warning. If someone told me to run, I'd leave the dough right where it sat.

The answer is that the LORD will strip Esau bare. He asks about grape gatherers and thieves, and then says, “But I will strip Esau bare…” Grape gatherers leave some gleanings and thieves take only what they want. This is far beyond either one. The “But” marks the turn.

The answer is False. The LORD says, “I will uncover his hiding places, and he will be unable to conceal himself.” His hiding places get uncovered. He can't hide, and that's the whole point of the verse.

The answer is preserve. The LORD says, “Abandon your orphans; I will preserve their lives.” Right in the middle of a heavy passage, there's a promise to keep orphans alive. I think that's a tender thing to find here, friends.

The answer is True. The LORD asks, “If those who do not deserve to drink the cup must drink it, can you possibly remain unpunished?” Then He says, “You will not go unpunished, for you must drink it too.” The verse says Edom drinks the cup too.

The answer is that He swears by Himself. The LORD says, “For by Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD…” That's the highest kind of oath there is. Scripture says that when God made His promise to Abraham, He had no one greater to swear by, so He swore by Himself (Hebrews 6:13).
The answer is False. The LORD says, “…all her cities will be in ruins forever.” Forever doesn't leave room for a short while. I think this one is a heavy moment, and the text doesn't soften it.

The answer is assemble and rise up for battle. The envoy's message is, “Assemble yourselves to march against her! Rise up for battle!” The nations are being called to gather and march against Edom. It's a call to arms, not a call to a party.

The answer is pride. The LORD says, “The terror you cause and the pride of your heart have deceived you…” Pride can fool a person right out of their senses. I've been fooled by my own pride more than once, mostly about how straight I was pressing.

The answer is that He will bring Edom down from there. The LORD says, “Though you elevate your nest like the eagle, even from there I will bring you down,” declares the LORD. A nest up high feels safe, but height doesn't stop Him. Edom's high place doesn't change the outcome.

The answer is True. The LORD says, “Edom will become an object of horror. All who pass by will be appalled and will scoff at all her wounds.” I think this part is heavy, friends. Those passing by are appalled, and they scoff.

The answer is Sodom and Gomorrah, two cities that were overthrown (Genesis 19:24-25). The LORD says, “As Sodom and Gomorrah were overthrown along with their neighbors… no one will dwell there; no man will abide there.” That's the comparison He picks for Edom's future. It's a heavy one.

The answer is False. The LORD asks, “For who is like Me, and who can challenge Me? What shepherd can stand against Me?” The questions answer themselves. No one is like Him, and no shepherd can stand against Him.

The answer is False. The verse speaks of the plans the LORD has drawn up against Edom, and then says, “Surely the little ones of the flock will be dragged away; certainly their pasture will be made desolate because of them.” They aren't kept safe. It's a heavy line, friends, and I won't pretend otherwise.

The answer is quake. The passage says, “At the sound of their fall the earth will quake; their cry will resound to the Red Sea.” The earth shakes at the sound of the fall. The cry carries all the way to the Red Sea.

The answer is the heart of a woman in labor. The passage says, “In that day the hearts of Edom’s mighty men will be like the heart of a woman in labor.” These are the mighty men, and their hearts are anything but mighty. Notice the word “like.” It's a comparison, and the text doesn't say more than that.
